FACTOR_G.label: Factor causing growth: rise in government spending (G)

FACTOR_I.label: Factor causing growth: rise in investment (I)

FACTOR_LABOUR_QTY.label: Factor causing growth: increase in the quantity of labour (workforce size, immigration, participation)

FACTOR_LABOUR_QUALITY.label: Factor causing growth: increase in the quality of labour (education, training, human capital)

FACTOR_TECH.label: Factor causing growth: technological progress and innovation raising productivity

FACTOR_LAND.label: Factor causing growth: increase in quantity/exploitation of natural resources

TRADE_SPECIALISATION.label: Specialising in production of goods/services to trade

NX_COMP.label: Net trade (X-M) as a component of AD

stages.name: Economic growth
stages.title: Economic growth
stages.sub: Distinguish actual growth from potential growth and see how they combine into the long-term trend rate.

steps.q: A country's shoppers spend more this year and its factories sell more goods abroad than last year. Together, could these push actual output up?
steps.right: Yes, both add to spending on domestically made goods
steps.wrong: No, only spending at home counts towards output
steps.hint: Exports are goods sold abroad, but they are still made and counted at home.

steps.q: Last year a country produced £900bn of real output. This year it produced £918bn. What has just been measured?
steps.right: The percentage change in actual output over the year
steps.wrong: The maximum output the country could ever produce
steps.hint: £900bn to £918bn is what actually got made, not the ceiling on what could be made.

steps.q: A country's factories start selling far more abroad, earning foreign currency that funds new equipment and skills at home. Could this raise the country's ability to produce, not just this year's spending?
steps.right: Yes, trade earnings can raise capacity to produce
steps.wrong: No, selling abroad only affects the current year's spending
steps.hint: Money earned from exports does not have to be spent straight away, it can also fund new capacity.

steps.q: A country builds more factories and trains more workers, so the maximum it could sustainably produce rises, even before it actually produces more. What has changed?
steps.right: The economy's productive capacity has grown
steps.wrong: The economy's actual output this year has grown
steps.hint: This is about the ceiling on what could be made, not what was actually made this year.

steps.q: Some years actual growth is high, other years it is low, as spending swings up and down. But the economy's capacity has been rising steadily for decades. What best describes that steady long-run rate?
steps.right: The average sustainable growth rate over the long run
steps.wrong: Whatever the actual growth rate happens to be this year
steps.hint: Think about smoothing out the ups and downs of actual growth to see the underlying path of capacity.
